rationale: Abstract 9 reports a lower-range TBP expansion with a Lewy-like phenotype and visual hallucinations. Abstract 50 describes a distinct case with autoimmune features, and abstract 96 reports TARDBP-related atypical parkinsonism. Their clinical signs are separate from any treatment or nutrient observation. The proceedings contain no measured dried fig exposure with visual episode counts.

The complete meeting supplement contains separate reports of visual hallucinations attributed to an occipital stroke and possible checkpoint-inhibitor encephalitis. Other members discuss nutritional deficiencies and general nutritional care in different patients. There is no named dried fig exposure or food-timed Parkinson hallucination comparison.

The proceedings describe a varicella patient with altered behavior and visual hallucinations in a differential between viral encephalitis and acyclovir neurotoxicity. This is a critical-care clinical report with a nonculinary exposure and no Parkinson visual episode-frequency series.

The analysis uses data from two cohorts totaling 88 Parkinson participants and relates motor and nonmotor network connectivity to off-medication motor examination scores. Visual-network involvement predicts a motor outcome and supplies no evidence about food-timed visual hallucinations.

Postmortem pathological findings and clinical neuropsychiatric symptoms are compared across frontotemporal lobar degeneration categories. The pathologic phenotype includes behavioral measures instead of a dried fig exposure or longitudinal Parkinson visual endpoint.

The review describes dementia-associated clinical features and candidate management approaches across disorders. Visual hallucinations are a prognostic or diagnostic feature in the discussion. The paper does not present an original dried fig or episode-frequency comparison.

The systematic review follows reports of mania and related syndromes across dementia diagnoses and summarizes pharmacologic and clinical context. It does not measure dried fig intake or recurrent visual hallucination frequency in Parkinson disease.

Researchers summarize distinct pharmacologic exposures and harms in substance use disorder studies. The review mentions experimental mechanisms of potential neurological interest. The ingested substance and populations do not match dried fig or Parkinson visual episode frequency.

This review examines genetic variation in medication response and adverse effects, particularly with levodopa. The comparisons concern drug-specific pharmacogenomics without an observed dried fig exposure, timing, or visual episode count.

The treatment review separates changes in daily off time from medication adverse events such as visual hallucinations. Medication-related occurrence does not measure hallucination frequency after dietary fig intake.

This review explains diagnostic imaging patterns and markers across neurodegenerative syndromes. Clinical hallucinations are among the dementia with Lewy bodies criteria. The imaged phenotype supplies no timed culinary exposure contrast.

The pilot measures selected neuropsychological domains in methylmalonic and propionic acidemia to inform potential trials. The metabolic conditions and measured tests differ from habitual fig intake and recurrent visual hallucinations in Parkinson disease.

The structural imaging analysis distinguishes data-driven atrophy patterns in dementia with Lewy bodies and compares their clinical profiles. The subtypes are grouped by imaging and diagnosis, with no dried fig intervention or prospective visual episode frequency outcome.

The clinical comparison includes Parkinson disease with cognitive impairment, Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia. It relates Neuropsychiatric Inventory outcomes to caregiver distress and other clinical variables. Those domain ratings are separate from counted visual episodes after eating dried figs.

The imaging study compares subregional dopaminergic findings in 123 probable dementia with Lewy bodies participants and 78 controls. Imaging outcomes and clinical phenotype by sex are separate from a culinary exposure and a visual episode-frequency outcome.

The clinical review distinguishes reversible and degenerative causes of ataxia. Visual hallucinations appear in differential diagnostic criteria, including their timing in multiple system atrophy. There is no tested dried fig exposure.

The study examines cerebral glucose metabolism and nigrostriatal degeneration in isolated REM sleep behavior disorder. Imaging and prodromal clinical measurements do not record dried fig intake or visual hallucinatory effects after a meal.

The review examines tripartite motif proteins across neurological diseases. It discusses characteristic Lewy body symptoms while reviewing cell or tissue findings. No comparison of ingested dried figs or food-timed visual episodes is reported.

The authors inspect registered trials whose outcomes concern cognitive impairment in Parkinson disease. The review's treatment and endpoint mapping supplies no dried fig exposure or separate visual episode-frequency result.

The review identifies 12 heterogeneous low-carbohydrate or ketogenic studies with incomplete reporting of carbohydrate exposure. Mood or anxiety outcomes in these diet comparisons do not establish that dried fig was tested or that Parkinson visual hallucinations changed.

Conflicting sensorimotor stimulation examines sensed presence among different Parkinson symptom groups. In the four phantom-boarder cases, three reported complex visual hallucinations, separately from phantom-boarder episodes. The experiment neither changes food intake nor records visual episodes after dried figs.

The review discusses gastrointestinal symptoms, physiology and management in Parkinson and related Lewy body disorders. Its nutrition and visual hallucination mentions address different clinical issues. No food-timed dried fig or recurrent visual outcome comparison is published.

Participants undergo visual and verbal memory testing over follow-up. The DMS48 reflects recognition memory and is distinct from experiencing a visual hallucination. The report does not identify food exposure.

The study compares lithium regimens in 16 Parkinson participants and records biomarker, safety and imaging measures. The intervention is medication and no culinary fig exposure or Parkinson visual episode-frequency comparison appears.

Clinical ratings, recorded gait and structural MRI are compared in 16 Caribbean atypical parkinsonism cases, 15 PSP cases and 17 controls. The study does not track dried figs or the frequency of visual episodes.

The multicenter classification study compares structural imaging across Parkinson psychosis and schizophrenia categories. Hallucinations contribute to broad clinical grouping; no dried fig ingestion or timed visual outcomes are measured.

The DLB and mild cognitive impairment imaging analysis relates lower regional dopamine transporter uptake to recorded hallucination status and other clinical features. Association with occurrence is distinct from change in episode frequency after eating, and food exposure is not measured.

Case 2 had a low serum magnesium concentration, cerebellar edema and delirium with visual hallucinations. Overall symptoms improved after intravenous magnesium, withdrawal of antiviral medication and prior thiamine treatment. Later low magnesium recurred with ataxia and no reported cognitive symptoms. Dried figs contain measured magnesium, but the case has no Parkinson diagnosis, food exposure or separately timed episode frequency.

The review examines representation, recognition and symptom reporting in Lewy body dementia. Informant differences and clinical hallucination reporting do not provide a dried fig comparison or food-timed outcome.

The commentary interprets the same Okkels cohort published under DOI 10.1093/brain/awad192. It describes no clear cholinergic PET difference by hallucination status. The commentary is a derivative report, and neither gives an oral dried fig contrast.

The analysis compares neuropsychological profiles across 168 Alzheimer and 169 Lewy body dementia participants. The test scores and diagnostic groups supply no food exposure or measure of visual hallucination episode change.

The cross-sectional study evaluates SARC-F and calf circumference against a sarcopenia reference assessment. It does not measure dried fig consumption or repeated visual hallucinations during a defined dietary interval.

The investigators assay 172 baseline plasma samples, with repeated samples in 55. The second recruitment cohort uses the previously reported cardiac MIBG method, and a prior p-tau181 result is reused. Visual hallucinations are rated as present or absent for clinical classification, without a dried fig exposure.

A spastic paraplegia type 30 case describes well-formed visual hallucinations that later settled without treatment for the hallucinations. The clinical phenotype and medication history do not include dried fig intake or a counted interval for visual episodes.

The postmortem study examines alpha-synuclein pathology in retinal and optic nerve tissue across diagnoses. Histopathology offers an ocular biomarker contrast without food exposure or measured visual episode change.

Investigators measure hundreds of CSF proteins to seek markers distinguishing disease groups. Clinical diagnostic criteria and proteomic differences are not measurements of dried fig intake or event frequency after eating.

The review examines intracranial signals related to mood and motivation in Parkinson disease. A cited recording series lists one participant with a visual hallucination, and relates the task to electrical signals. There is no dried fig or food timing comparison.

This review discusses cell states, pathways and possible therapeutic targets across neurodegeneration. Recurrent visual hallucinations are described as a clinical DLB feature without experimental measurement of oral dried figs.

The experiment manipulates expectation cues and measures stimulus-specific activity across cortical layers. The induced false percept task is not a Parkinson food-exposure study and does not follow spontaneous visual hallucinations after meals.

The prospective cohort combines smell testing, cognitive and motor assessments and MRI over follow-up. The olfactory and structural outcomes do not test dried figs or record visual hallucinations in relation to food intake.

The systematic review separates off-time trials, selected patients with existing hallucinations, and observational worsening reports. A TOLEDO extension follows the same trial family. The therapy is subcutaneous medication and the review has no dried fig comparison.

The original reports any psychotic features in 27 of 70 early Parkinson participants and three of 74 controls. The 10PDQ identifies sensory type separately from frequency of the worst psychotic experience, and CAARMS scores combine frequency and duration. The study does not track dried fig intake or separately count visual episodes after meals.

The network meta-analysis compares randomized drug treatments for Parkinson motor fluctuations and adverse events. Hallucination reporting is drug-related and event definitions vary. It is not a dried fig or clinical visual episode-frequency intervention.

The article describes two additional SNCA multiplication cases and compares findings across earlier publications. Psychiatric features belong to genetic and medication histories. No reported comparison links dried fig consumption to visual episode frequency.

The study compares FDG PET metabolic network patterns in people with extracranial diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and controls. The abbreviation DLBCL identifies a malignancy and does not denote Lewy body disease. There is no fig or Parkinson visual comparison.

The narrative review discusses uses of mirtazapine and individual reports of drug-related perceptual changes, including a visual hallucination case. These reports concern medication effects and provide no dried fig exposure or recurrent visual episode-rate comparison.

The review describes clinical features, pathology markers, genetic factors and imaging across Lewy body disorders. Visual hallucinations are used as phenotype context, with no assessed dried fig exposure or food-timed events.

The study focuses on FDG PET metabolic networks in 22 probable or possible DLB participants with little evidence of dopamine transporter loss. Metabolic classification provides no dietary contrast, visual episode count or association with dried figs.

The review investigates olfactory cells as a model to study pathways implicated in schizophrenia. Discussion of visual hallucinations and transmitter drugs is secondary disease context. No culinary fig or clinical visual outcome is measured.

The paper discusses waking versus sleep-transition perceptual experiences, including common Parkinson descriptions. Its conceptual definitions support phenotyping and do not test dried figs or count visual episodes relative to eating.

The review compares radiotracer methods and disease imaging patterns across forms of parkinsonism. The visual hallucination discussion describes reported metabolic associations without an oral dried fig exposure or associated episode frequency.
